subject: chemistry
title: Concentration in mol/dm³
key_idea: Concentration can be measured in mol/dm³ as well as g/dm³. Moles of solute = concentration × volume in dm³. Multiply mol/dm³ by Mr to get g/dm³, and divide g/dm³ by Mr to get mol/dm³.

blocks.text: (Higher tier, chemistry only) Concentration can be given as the amount of solute in moles in each dm³ of solution. This links the mass of solute and the volume of solution through the number of moles.

blocks.label: Concentration in mol/dm³
blocks.formula: concentration = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution
where: moles of solute is in mol
volume of solution is in dm³

blocks.text: Example: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.100 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.0025 mol of solute.

items: Moles = concentration × volume (dm³). Divide cm³ by 1000 first.

blocks.text: (Higher tier, chemistry only) Moles and mass are linked by the relative formula mass, so concentrations are linked in the same way.

blocks.label: From mol/dm³ to g/dm³
where: Mr is the relative formula mass of the solute

where: Mr is the relative formula mass of the solute

blocks.text: A copper sulfate solution has a concentration of 15.95 g/dm³. Mr of CuSO₄ = 159.5. Calculate the moles in 50.0 cm³.

diagram.question: A solution of sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, has a concentration of **{c}** mol/dm³. Calculate its concentration in g/dm³. Mr of H₂SO₄ = 98.
working: Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × Mr.

items: Multiply by Mr to go from mol/dm³ to g/dm³.
Divide by Mr to go from g/dm³ to mol/dm³.

sections.heading: Making a solution and using reacting volumes

blocks.text: (Higher tier, chemistry only) The amount in moles, or the mass of solute, in a given volume can be calculated from the concentration.
Example: to make 250 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate (Mr = 106), moles = 0.100 × 0.250 = 0.0250 mol, so the mass is 0.0250 × 106 = 2.65 g.

items: If two solutions react completely, and the volumes and one concentration are known, the other concentration can be found.
Work out the moles of the known solution, use the equation ratio, then divide by the volume of the unknown solution.
This is how titration results are used (see titration calculations).
Moles of solute = concentration × volume. Mass = moles × Mr.
Use the equation ratio to move from one solution to another.

checks.q: Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide in 20.0 cm³ of a 0.500 mol/dm³ solution.
A solution of sodium hydroxide has a concentration of 0.25 mol/dm³. Calculate its concentration in g/dm³. Mr of NaOH = 40.
A solution of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 7.3 g/dm³. Mr of HCl = 36.5. Calculate its concentration in mol/dm³.

mistakes.wrong: Moles of acid = 15.0 × 0.0480 = 0.72, because the volume is 15.0 cm³.
mistakes.right: Divide the volume by 1000 to get dm³ before multiplying: 15.0 ÷ 1000 × 0.0480 = 0.00072 mol.

mistakes.wrong: Moles of NaOH = moles of acid, so concentration = 0.00072 ÷ 25.0 × 1000 = 0.0288 mol/dm³.
mistakes.right: Use the ratio in the equation. 1 mol of H₂C₂O₄ reacts with 2 mol of NaOH, so the moles of NaOH are 0.00144. Use of an incorrect mole ratio loses the ratio mark.
The volume must be in dm³. Concentration = 0.00144 × 1000 ÷ 25.0 = 0.0576 mol/dm³.

worked_example.question:
A student found that 25.0 cm³ of a sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by 15.00 cm³ of 0.0480 mol/dm³ ethanedioic acid solution.

The equation for the reaction is:
H₂C₂O₄ + 2 NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2 H₂O

Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm³.
worked_example.tip: One mark each: moles of acid, the 1 : 2 ratio, then the concentration.

exam_phrases: moles acid = ½ x moles alkali

mistakes.right: Check the size of the answer. 98 × 0.250 = 24.5 g/dm³. A slip in the decimal place scores only 1 of the 2 marks.

mistakes.wrong: Moles of H₂SO₄ = 2 × moles of NaOH, giving 0.388 mol/dm³.
mistakes.right: The equation is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH, so the acid has half the moles of the alkali. Multiply by ½ to give 0.097 mol/dm³.

mistakes.wrong: Concentration of H₂SO₄ = 24.25 × 0.200 ÷ 25.00 = 0.194 mol/dm³, with no ½.
mistakes.right: Use the ratio in the equation. Moles of acid = ½ × moles of alkali, which gives 0.097 mol/dm³.

worked_example.question:
The copper sulfate solution used has a concentration of 15.95 g dm⁻³.

Calculate the number of moles of copper sulfate, CuSO₄, in 50.00 cm³ of this solution.
(relative atomic masses: O = 16, S = 32, Cu = 63.5)
answer_points: Mass of copper sulfate = 50 ÷ 1000 × 15.95 = 0.7975 g, so moles = 0.7975 ÷ 159.5 = 0.005 mol.
Or: concentration = 15.95 ÷ 159.5 = 0.1 mol dm⁻³, so moles = 50 ÷ 1000 × 0.1 = 0.005 mol.
worked_example.tip: Either route scores. 0.005 mol scores all three marks, even without working.

exam_phrases: Conversion of cm³ to dm³: 25 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³

mistakes.wrong: Mass = concentration × volume, with the volume left in cm³.
mistakes.right: Convert the volume from cm³ to dm³ first (divide by 1000), or convert the concentration to g/cm³.

mistakes.wrong: To make 0.100 mol/dm³, dissolve 10.6 g in 1.0 dm³ of water.
mistakes.right: The concentration depends on the volume of the solution, not the volume of water. Dissolve the solute in water, then make up to 1.0 dm³ of solution.

mistakes.wrong: 0.100 mol/dm³ of sodium carbonate needs 106 g in 1.0 dm³.
mistakes.right: 106 g is 1 mol, which gives 1.00 mol/dm³. For 0.100 mol, the mass is 0.100 × 106 = 10.6 g.

worked_example.question:
Which of the following procedures is the most suitable for preparing a 0.100 mol/dm³ solution of sodium carbonate?

The relative formula mass, Mr, of sodium carbonate is 106.

A  Dissolving 10.6 g of sodium carbonate in water to make 1.0 dm³ of solution.
B  Dissolving 10.6 g of sodium carbonate in 0.10 dm³ of water.
C  Dissolving 10.6 g of sodium carbonate in 1.0 dm³ of water.
D  Dissolving 106 g of sodium carbonate in water to make 1.0 dm³ of solution.
answer_points: The mass is dissolved in water and made up to 1.0 dm³ of solution, so the answer is A.
worked_example.tip: The volume that counts is the volume of the solution, not the volume of water added.
